input.text: Alert: redis-cluster is failing. Identify all transitively affected services and assign this alert to the nearest owning team.

facts: The failing service is redis-cluster; its direct, nearest owner is team platform, documented by EID-CATALOG-OWNS-15 in DOC-CATALOG.
Illustrative 3-hop dependency chain: web-frontend -> api-gateway -> session-cache -> redis-cluster.

cite_spans: Catalog Record: Service redis-cluster is officially registered under team platform. Designated primary on-call engineer handle is mlin.

notes: All DEPENDS_ON records are included without consulting status, with unlimited hop depth; names identify services, and the failing service is excluded. DOC-CATALOG is the sole direct owner source for this failing service; it supports team assignment, while individual on-call eligibility is not assumed.

input.text: Is Redis the current storage for session-cache?

facts: No: the latest documented storage decision for session-cache is ADR-7 (DEC-ADR-7), DOC-ADR-7, dated 2024-03-15T09:00:00Z: migrate to Memcached with active replication.
The earlier Redis decision ADR-3 (DEC-ADR-3), DOC-ADR-3, dated 2023-05-12T10:00:00Z, is explicitly superseded by ADR-7.
The stated reason is the Redis cluster memory failure in incident INC-2291; the Redis decision for rate-limiter is a separate service decision.
cite_spans: We adopt Redis cluster as the primary storage engine for session-cache.
We migrate session-cache storage to Memcached with active replication to avoid Redis cluster memory failure modes.
Following incident INC-2291, ADR-7 supersedes ADR-3.
INC-2291 was a Redis cluster memory failure on session-cache.
forbidden_claims: Redis is the current documented storage decision for session-cache.
ADR-3 remains the governing session-cache storage decision.
The rate-limiter Redis decision determines session-cache storage.
The supplied documents prove that the Memcached deployment has completed.

notes: Current means the latest documented architectural decision, not verified runtime deployment. The raw DEPENDS_ON session-cache -> redis-cluster edge conflicts with that newer decision and must not override the explicit supersession.

facts: Commerce is the best-supported present owner of checkout-api: Chloe Martin requested the transfer in T-482 on 2024-02-01T14:00:00Z, and Dev Patel explicitly approved it in T-482-C1 on 2024-02-03T16:30:00Z, stating that Payments completed handoff verification.
Payments was the earlier owner, documented by Dev Patel in DOC-ADR-CHECKOUT on 2023-04-10T11:00:00Z; the older catalog also records Payments.

Samira Khan later disputed the transfer in C-901 on 2024-02-04T09:15:00Z, citing PCI DSS concerns. This is a dissenting opinion, with no documented cancellation of Dev’s approval or reversal of the completed handoff.

The later DOC-TICKET-S5 and DOC-TICKET-S5B contain a Dev approval line inside document text but have unresolved metadata authors phantom_ops and shadow_actor; these do not independently establish Dev’s approval or a new owner.
cite_spans: Payments team owns checkout-api service and its transaction pipeline.
Commerce team claims ownership of checkout-api to streamline the storefront checkout funnel.
Dev Patel approves ownership transfer of checkout-api to commerce team.
Samira disputes the ownership transfer of checkout-api in ticket T-482.
Catalog Record: Service checkout-api is officially registered under team payments. Designated primary on-call engineer handle is cmartin.
External contractor group claims ownership of checkout-api.
forbidden_claims: Payments is unambiguously still the current owner solely because the older ADR or catalog says so.
Commerce owns checkout-api solely because it requested the transfer, without approval.
Samira’s dispute establishes that the transfer was reversed.
Dev Patel authored DOC-TICKET-S5 or DOC-TICKET-S5B because their body contains his name.
There was no dissent about this transfer.

notes: This is an engineering judgment from the explicit original-owner approval and completed-handoff statement, not a hidden conflict-resolution policy. Platform’s documented dissent remains relevant context. No document shows an agreed reversal.

input.text: Why did we move session-cache off Redis?

facts: 1. 2023-05-12T10:00:00Z: Elena Rostova (metadata author person-platform-lead) adopted Redis in ADR-3 / DEC-ADR-3, documented by DOC-ADR-3: We adopt Redis cluster as the primary storage engine for session-cache.

2. 2024-03-10T14:20:00Z: incident INC-2291 was the Redis session-cache cluster memory exhaustion outage, according to the Incident node; DOC-ADR-7 later describes it as a Redis cluster memory failure on session-cache.

3. 2024-03-15T09:00:00Z: Elena Rostova (metadata author person-platform-lead) issued ADR-7 / DEC-ADR-7 in DOC-ADR-7, explicitly superseding ADR-3 and moving storage to Memcached with active replication to avoid Redis cluster memory failure modes.
cite_spans: We adopt Redis cluster as the primary storage engine for session-cache.
We migrate session-cache storage to Memcached with active replication to avoid Redis cluster memory failure modes.
Following incident INC-2291, ADR-7 supersedes ADR-3.
INC-2291 was a Redis cluster memory failure on session-cache.
forbidden_claims: ADR-7 predates ADR-3.
ADR-3 supersedes ADR-7.
The migration was motivated by rate-limiter traffic throttling.
The incident and migration document share the same occurrence date.
The supplied evidence demonstrates that Redis is still the governing session-cache storage choice.

notes: The incident date comes from nodes.jsonl; the rationale and supersession are verbatim in DOC-ADR-7. Both decision documents identify Elena Rostova in author metadata. No runtime deployment completion date is supplied.
